claims.text: The coupled tribo-corrosion response of high-entropy alloys is governed by the balance between mechanical removal of the passive oxide film and its regeneration.
When mechanical wear exceeds the passive-film regeneration rate, the protective barrier is compromised.
Compromise of the passive film exposes fresh metal to corrosive attack.
Wear-induced exposure of fresh metal produces a synergistic increase in overall degradation.
Controlled heat treatment and atmospheric exposure can produce a homogeneous high-entropy-alloy microstructure with an in-situ self-passivating oxide layer.
Cr-, Al-, or similarly enriched oxides can provide self-passivation in the proposed alloy.
Varying contact load or sliding speed while holding electrolyte conditions constant will modulate wear intensity and isolate the effect of passive-film removal.
Static conditions allow the passive film to remain intact or reform and thereby limit degradation.
A critical wear threshold exists above which abrasion-corrosion coupling increases the degradation rate.
Higher mechanical wear will cause greater total degradation than matched static-corrosion and wear-only baselines.
Higher mechanical wear will increase corrosion rates, observable as higher electrochemical current densities.
Higher mechanical wear will increase wear volume.
The prediction should hold for alloys that form a robust, self-healing passive film.
The prediction may fail when the passive film is inherently unstable or when temperature alters film-formation kinetics.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply at moderate temperatures and neutral pH where a self-healing passive oxide readily forms.
The proposed mechanism may not govern when alloy passivation is poor or mechanical loading is too low to disrupt the film.
Microstructural heterogeneities can interact with local corrosion behavior and complicate the tribo-corrosion response.
